cldc.caption: Civil Liberties Defense Center — the organisation that issued this release.
cldc.why: Fifteen press releases republished from cldc.org, none of which carries a photograph on cldc.org either. The issuing organisations own mark on its own release: unambiguous, impossible to mistake for event photography, no licensing risk, and it visually groups the CLDC republications as the set they are. Sourced from cldc.org and set on a plain card rather than hotlinked.

individual.caption: An “ICE Out of Our Schools” protest in New York City. Photograph by SWinxy, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Illustrative of the policy this article describes; not of any individual named in it.
individual.why: Student visa revocations aimed at campus protest. The nearest freely licensed photograph of the thing itself.

individual.caption: Stop Cop City march, Atlanta, January 2023. Photograph by Tatsoi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
individual.why: The essay is about the Weelaunee forest movement and the Georgia jails that followed it. This is that movement, in that city, in that period.

individual.caption: An anti-ICE protest sign in Minneapolis. Photograph by Chad Davis, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Illustrative; not from the Cities Church protest.
individual.why: Minnesota anti-ICE protest imagery for a Minnesota anti-ICE prosecution. The caption says plainly that it is not the event itself.

individual.caption: Panther 21 rally at Hunter College, New York. Photograph by Bill Andrews, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. The movement Johanna Fernández spent her career documenting — not a photograph of her.
individual.why: No freely licensed portrait of her could be found, and an obituary should not carry a picture that pretends to be the person. This is the New York movement history she wrote, captioned as exactly that.

individual.caption: U.S. Department of Justice headquarters, Washington, D.C. CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
individual.why: An arrest abroad on U.S. federal charges. He is in this archive as a prisoner but has no photograph on his record, and a stand-in face would be worse than none. The prosecuting institution is the honest subject.

individual.caption: Wetʼsuwetʼen solidarity rally, San Francisco, February 7, 2020. Photograph by Peg Hunter, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
individual.why: The article is specifically about U.S. solidarity defendants. This is a U.S. solidarity action for the same struggle.

individual.caption: The NPPC political-prisoner database — what the app puts in a pocket.
individual.why: NPPCs own screen, own work. The release announces an app that does not exist to photograph yet, so it shows the thing the app carries rather than a mock-up of a product.

individual.caption: Eugene V. Debs speaking at Canton, Ohio, June 16, 1918 — the speech that brought his Espionage Act prosecution. Photograph by James V. McCann, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
individual.why: Not illustrative but literal: this photograph is of the speech that produced the most famous Espionage Act conviction in American history.

individual.caption: Thurgood Marshall United States Courthouse, New York. Photograph by Kidfly182, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
individual.why: An essay on political trials and political defense, over the federal courthouse where such trials are held.

decision_note: The curator asked me to choose, so: organisational mark for the organisations own releases, freely licensed photographs for everything else, and no licensed news photography anywhere. Nothing here costs money, nothing needs permission, and every third-party image carries its author and licence in the image_caption field rather than in a file nobody reads.
attribution_note: Attribution is stored on the article, not in a credits file. Six of the nine individual images are Creative Commons and legally require credit at the point of use; image_caption renders under the photograph, which is the point of use. Two are public domain and are credited anyway. Do not blank these captions.
honesty_note: Three captions say outright that the photograph is not of the event or person described — the Minneapolis sign, the Panther 21 rally standing in for Johanna Fernández, and the schools protest for the visa revocations. An illustrative photograph is fine; an illustrative photograph a reader mistakes for documentary evidence is not, and this archive is in the business of the difference.
wilansky_note: Still not used, and the reason has not changed: the court-exhibit photographs of Sophia Wilanskys destroyed arm on the CLDC post are medical evidence of an open wound, and putting one in the /news thumbnail grid unannounced is a decision for a person, not a batch. The North Dakota release gets the CLDC mark like the rest.
